title: Superconductivity: When Resistance Vanishes Altogether
text:
In nineteen eleven, Kamerlingh Onnes was measuring how the electrical resistance of mercury changed as he cooled it towards absolute zero. What he expected was a gradual decline, and there was good reason to expect it: resistance arises largely from electrons scattering off the thermal vibrations of the crystal lattice, and cooling reduces those vibrations. What he found was not gradual at all. A few degrees above absolute zero the resistance did not merely fall, it vanished, abruptly and completely, at a sharply defined temperature.

That is superconductivity, and it is not simply very good conduction. In a superconducting ring, a current once started will circulate without any measurable decay. The explanation took several decades to arrive. Below the critical temperature, electrons stop behaving as independent particles; they pair up, through distortions of the lattice itself, and those pairs move collectively in a single quantum state that the lattice cannot scatter one electron at a time.

There is a second signature worth remembering. A superconductor expels magnetic fields from its interior, which is why a magnet can be made to hover steadily above one. The obstacle to using any of this widely is temperature, and raising the critical temperature remains a central problem of the field.
points: Kamerlingh Onnes cooled mercury towards absolute zero expecting resistance to fall gradually.
Resistance normally comes from electrons scattering off lattice vibrations, which cooling reduces.
Instead the resistance vanished completely and abruptly at a sharp critical temperature.
A current in a superconducting ring persists without measurable decay, so this is not merely good conduction.
Below the critical temperature electrons pair up via lattice distortions and move as one quantum state that cannot be scattered individually.
Superconductors also expel magnetic fields, allowing magnetic levitation, and raising the critical temperature is still the main obstacle.
